hints: Notice the time for one oscillation on the original displacement-time graph and check which option keeps that same period, since frequency remains constant.
Recall that for a wave $I \propto A^2$, so halving intensity does not halve the displacement amplitude.
Calculate the new amplitude as $A_{new} = A/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.71A$ and look for the same-period graph with peaks about 70% as tall.
walkthrough: The original graph shows displacement against time. The time period $T$ is the time for one full oscillation and frequency is $f = 1/T$.
Frequency remains constant, so $T$ must stay the same. Only the graph with the same number of oscillations in the same time as the original can be correct.
Intensity of a progressive wave is proportional to amplitude squared: $I \propto A^2$ for constant frequency.
Halving intensity gives $I_{new} = I/2$, so $A_{new}^2 = A^2/2$ and $A_{new} = A/\sqrt{2} \approx 0.71A$.
The new displacement-time graph must therefore have the same period but peaks about 0.7 times the original height, not half height.

A.explanation: Amplitude is unchanged and period is halved, so frequency is doubled, not constant as required.

B.explanation: Period is doubled so frequency is halved, and amplitude is unchanged, so intensity is unchanged, not halved.

C.explanation: Period is doubled so frequency is halved, and amplitude is halved which would make intensity one quarter, not one half.

D.explanation: Period is unchanged so frequency is constant, and amplitude is reduced by factor $1/\sqrt{2}$, so $I \propto A^2$ is halved.
